1010:
Before understanding what this idiom means, picture the physical image it comes from.

Imagine you are standing on a street. There is a building or a bend in the road in front of you. You cannot see what is on the other side yet — but it is very close. It is just around the corner. You only need to take a few more steps, and you will reach it.

This image is the heart of the idiom.
What the Idiom Actually Means

When people say something is "around the corner," they mean it is going to happen very soon. It is not here yet, but it is so close that it feels almost visible — just like something physically sitting around the bend of a road.

It is used to talk about time, not physical distance.

Simple definition: Something is "around the corner" when it is about to happen in the very near future.
How the Literal Connects to the Figurative

Think of it this way:

  • Physical corner → something is nearby in space
  • Idiomatic corner → something is nearby in time

The leap from space to time is natural. In everyday life, we often describe time using the language of space. We say "the future is ahead of us," "the past is behind us," or "a big event is coming." The idiom "around the corner" follows the same logic — if something is just around the corner, it is right there, almost within reach, just not quite here yet.
Examples in Sentences

Here are examples across different situations so you can see how naturally this idiom appears:

Seasons and Holidays:

  • "Winter is just around the corner — you should buy a warm coat soon."
  • "Christmas is around the corner, so the shops are getting very busy."

Personal life:

  • "Don't give up. Success is just around the corner."
  • "Her graduation is right around the corner — her family is already planning a party."

Business and Economy:

  • "Economists are saying that a recovery is around the corner."
  • "The launch of our new product is right around the corner."

Warnings:

  • "Exams are around the corner, so stop wasting time."
  • "The deadline is around the corner — we need to hurry."

In every example above, notice that the thing being talked about has not happened yet, but it is very close in time.
The Word "Just" and "Right" — Why They Are Added

You will very often hear people say:

  • "just around the corner"
  • "right around the corner"

These words are added for emphasis. They make the idiom even stronger, pushing the idea that the event is extremely close — almost here this very moment. Without these words, the idiom still works, but with them, the sense of urgency or nearness is stronger.

Think of it like this:

  • "Around the corner" = soon
  • "Just around the corner" = very soon, almost here
The Tone: Is It Always Positive?

No, not always. This is an important nuance.

Most of the time, the idiom is used for things that are positive or exciting — a holiday, a victory, a new beginning, spring after a long winter. The tone feels hopeful and encouraging.

Example: "Keep working hard — your breakthrough is just around the corner."

However, it can also be used neutrally or even negatively, especially when talking about something difficult or unwelcome that is approaching.

Example: "Don't relax yet — more trouble is around the corner."
Example: "Tax season is around the corner again."

So the idiom itself is neutral in nature — its positive or negative feeling comes entirely from what is said to be around the corner.
What the Idiom Does NOT Mean

It is important to be clear about what this idiom does not mean:

  • It does not mean something is physically near in location. If your friend says "the bakery is around the corner," they probably mean it literally — that is not the idiom. Context tells you which meaning is being used.
  • It does not mean something is already happening. The thing is still in the future, even if very close. The moment it arrives, you would no longer use this phrase.
  • It does not always mean something will happen today or tomorrow. "Soon" is relative. Depending on context, "around the corner" could mean next week, next month, or the next season — but it always implies closeness compared to a larger timeframe.
How to Tell the Literal From the Idiomatic

Since the same phrase can be literal or idiomatic, you need to look at context.

  • Literal: "Turn left, and the pharmacy is around the corner." → Talking about physical location.
  • Idiomatic: "Spring is just around the corner." → Spring cannot literally be around a corner. This is clearly about time.

When the subject is a time-based event, season, or change, it is almost always the idiom.
Similar Idioms With the Same Meaning

It helps to know expressions that mean the same thing, so you can recognize the idea even when different words are used:

  • "On the horizon" — something is approaching, visible in the distance (like the horizon line)
  • "In the pipeline" — something is being prepared and will arrive soon
  • "Imminent" — a formal single word meaning about to happen very soon
  • "Coming up" — a casual way to say something is approaching
  • "At hand" — something is very near and almost ready
  • "Any day now" — something could arrive at any moment

Among these, "around the corner" is one of the most visual and memorable because of the concrete image it creates in your mind.
A Simple Memory Trick

Every time you hear or read "around the corner," close your eyes and picture yourself standing on a street. Something wonderful (or important) is just out of sight — past the bend. You cannot see it yet, but you know it is there, right on the other side. Just a few more steps.

That picture is exactly what the idiom means in time: something is so close, you almost have it.
Quick Summary

ConceptDetail

"Around the corner" is an idiom meaning something is going to happen very soon. It comes from the image of something being physically close, just past a bend in the road. It is used for seasons, events, changes, successes, and even problems. Adding "just" or "right" makes the nearness feel even stronger. It can be positive, neutral, or slightly negative depending on what is said to be arriving. The thing described has not happened yet but is about to.
1011:
Arouse means to bring something that was inactive, hidden, or dormant into an active state — to "wake it up" and make it present and felt.

Think of it like a sleeping fire. The embers are there, but nothing is happening. Then something comes along and stirs those embers into a flame. That act of stirring — that's "arousing."

1. To cause a feeling, emotion, or reaction to emerge in someone

This is the most common and important use. When something arouses a feeling, it doesn't just create it casually — it stirs it up, pulls it out, makes it come alive in you.

"The documentary aroused deep sympathy in the audience."
"Her unusual behaviour aroused suspicion among her colleagues."
"The teacher's passion for the subject aroused genuine curiosity in the students."
"The unfair decision aroused anger among the workers."

Notice: the feeling wasn't fully there before. The documentary brought out sympathy. The behaviour brought out suspicion. That's what makes "arouse" precise — it always implies something being triggered or awakened from within.

The object of "arouse" in this sense is almost always an emotion or mental state:
curiosity, suspicion, interest, fear, anger, concern, passion, hostility, sympathy, excitement, anxiety, jealousy, hope, desire, wonder.

2. To cause sexual excitement or desire

This is a fully standard and dictionary-recognized meaning — not slang. When a person is aroused, they feel sexual desire or excitement.

"He found her completely arousing."
"She was aroused by his attention."

The noun form here is commonly used too: arousal (sexual arousal).

3. To wake someone from sleep (literary/formal)

This meaning exists and is historically important, though in modern everyday speech you'd more often hear "wake up" or "awaken." In formal writing, literature, or older texts, you'll still encounter it.

"She was aroused from a deep sleep by a loud bang outside."
"The smell of coffee aroused him from his drowsy state."

The idea connects back to the core meaning: pulling someone out of an inactive (sleeping) state into an active (awake) one.

4. To move someone into action; to stir them up

Sometimes "arouse" is used to mean prompting or energizing people to do something — especially when strong emotion is involved.

"The leader's speech aroused the crowd to demand justice."
"The injustice aroused the citizens into protest."

Arouse is a transitive verb — it almost always needs an object (something it acts on). You arouse something or someone. You don't just "arouse" on its own in standard usage.

The two most common structures:

① Something arouses [a feeling] in [a person]:

"The news aroused fear in everyone."
"The painting aroused wonder in those who saw it."

② Something/someone arouses [a person]:

"A sudden noise aroused her from sleep."
"The scene aroused him." (sexually)

Passive voice is very common:

"My curiosity was aroused."
"Suspicion was aroused by his evasive answers."
"She was aroused from her sleep."
The Key Nuance: Why "Arouse" and Not Just "Cause"?

You could theoretically say "the speech caused anger," but "arouse" says something richer.

"Arouse" carries these additional layers:

  • The feeling was latent — it existed as a potential within the person, and something brought it to the surface.
  • There's an element of intensity — aroused feelings are typically strong and vivid.
  • There's a sense of stirring — like waking something up, not just manufacturing something from nothing.

Compare:

"The film caused sadness." — plain, mechanical.
"The film aroused profound sadness in viewers." — richer; it stirred something deep within them.

This is why "arouse" pairs so naturally with words like suspicion, curiosity, and passion — these are things that lie beneath the surface and get pulled out.

Some feelings go especially naturally with "arouse." These pairings are so common in English that you should memorize them as natural phrases:

  • Arouse suspicion — perhaps the single most common collocation
  • Arouse curiosity
  • Arouse interest
  • Arouse concern
  • Arouse anger / fury / resentment
  • Arouse passion / desire
  • Arouse fear / anxiety
  • Arouse sympathy / compassion
  • Arouse hostility
  • Arouse emotions / feelings

"His secretive behaviour aroused suspicion."
"The unusual question aroused curiosity."
"The news aroused concern among health officials."

Understanding these differences will sharpen your sense of when to use "arouse."

Arouse vs. Evoke:
"Evoke" gently calls something up, often from memory or the imagination — it's softer and more reflective. "Arouse" is more forceful and active.

"The old photograph evoked nostalgia." (gentle recall)
"The injustice aroused outrage." (strong, forceful stirring)

Arouse vs. Provoke:
"Provoke" implies a more deliberate, often antagonistic challenge — there's almost always an edge of irritation or confrontation to it. "Arouse" is more neutral.

"His rudeness provoked her." (she was challenged/irritated into reacting)
"His story aroused her sympathy." (no confrontation, just a stirring of feeling)

Arouse vs. Incite:
"Incite" is stronger and almost always negative — it means pushing people toward violence, rebellion, or dangerous action.

"The speech incited the mob to riot." (deliberately pushing toward harmful action)
"The speech aroused strong emotions in the crowd." (neutral — just stirring feelings)

Arouse vs. Stimulate:
"Stimulate" is more neutral and clinical — you stimulate growth, stimulate the economy, stimulate a nerve. "Arouse" has more emotional and psychological depth.

"The drug stimulates the nervous system." (clinical)
"The film aroused my interest in history." (emotional/personal engagement)

Arouse vs. Kindle:
"Kindle" is more poetic and is typically used for positive feelings — hope, love, enthusiasm.

"Her encouragement kindled a love of reading in him." (warm, positive)
"The rumours aroused suspicion." — you wouldn't say "kindled suspicion."

"Arouse" is a slightly formal word — you'll hear it in writing, news, literature, formal speeches, and professional conversation. In casual everyday speech, people often use simpler alternatives:

Formal/WrittenCasual Speech

In formal contexts: "The incident aroused public concern."
In casual speech: "The incident got people worried."

Both are correct; "arouse" simply sounds more measured and precise, which is why it appears often in journalism, academic writing, and literature.

Arouse = to bring something dormant or inactive into a lively, active state.

Its most common use: to stir up a feeling, emotion, or reaction in someone — to make something that was hidden or quiet come alive and be felt strongly.

It also specifically means to cause sexual excitement, and in literary contexts, to wake someone from sleep.

The word always implies an agent (something doing the arousing) and a result (a feeling, state, or person that gets stirred into activity). It's more vivid and dynamic than simply "cause" — it suggests that something was lying beneath the surface and got pulled out, awakened, and activated.
1012: A chord is when two or more musical notes are played at the same time. For example, on a piano, if you press three keys simultaneously — say, C, E, and G — those three notes ring out together as one blended sound. That combined sound is a chord.

An arpeggio is what happens when, instead of playing all the notes of a chord at the same time, you play them one at a time, in quick flowing succession — either going upward (from the lowest note to the highest) or downward (from highest to lowest). The notes still belong to the same chord — you're simply spreading them out across a small stretch of time instead of hitting them all at once.

The simplest image: picture a harpist running their fingers across the strings. Each string rings out a split second after the last, creating a cascading, rippling wave of sound. That flowing, rolling quality is the essence of an arpeggio.

An arpeggio is also called a broken chord — and both terms mean exactly the same thing. "Broken" doesn't mean damaged; it means the chord has been broken apart, its notes separated in time rather than sounding all at once. You'll hear both terms used interchangeably in music.

An arpeggio can be:

  • Ascending — notes go from low to high (e.g., C → E → G)
  • Descending — notes go from high to low (e.g., G → E → C)
  • Both — up and then back down, or vice versa

The speed varies too. Sometimes the notes roll by so quickly the effect sounds almost like a single shimmering sound. Other times they're more deliberate and clearly separated. The defining feature stays the same regardless of speed: the notes of a chord, played one by one in sequence.

When a chord is played with all notes at once, it sounds solid and unified — one rich, full sound.

An arpeggio sounds more like flowing water, or a gentle wave. Imagine raindrops falling one after another into a still pond, each creating its own ripple. A regular chord is more like plunging your whole hand in at once — one big splash.

This rippling, lyrical quality is why arpeggios appear so often in romantic, emotional, or expressive music. They create a sense of movement and fluidity that block chords — all notes struck simultaneously — don't naturally have.

• Piano: A pianist rolls a chord — pressing the bottom note a fraction of a second before the others. This is one of the most iconic sounds in classical and romantic piano music.
  • Guitar: A guitarist picks through the individual strings of a chord one at a time, rather than strumming them all at once.
  • Harp: The harp is practically designed for arpeggios — sweeping a finger across the strings naturally produces that cascading effect.
  • Voice: Singers practice arpeggios by stepping through the notes of a chord one at a time, which trains their ear and strengthens their range.

Musicians — especially pianists and guitarists — practice "scales and arpeggios" as a daily technical exercise. This means playing through the chord-notes of many different chords, in sequence, up and down, across all the different musical keys. It builds finger strength, coordination, speed, and the kind of muscle memory that makes playing feel effortless.
Arpeggio vs. scale — what's the difference?

These two are mentioned together so often that it's worth being clear on how they differ.

A scale moves through every note in a musical key in step-by-step order. The C major scale, for instance, is: C – D – E – F – G – A – B – C. Nothing is skipped.

An arpeggio only uses the notes that belong to a specific chord — typically three or four notes — and skips everything in between. The C major arpeggio is just: C – E – G. (D, F, A, and B are skipped entirely.)

In short: a scale covers all the notes of a key; an arpeggio covers only the chord tones within that key.
How arpeggios look in written music

In sheet music, an arpeggio is shown as a wavy vertical line running alongside a chord. It tells the musician: don't play these notes all at once — roll through them from the bottom up (or sometimes top to bottom, shown with a downward arrow). This notation is called an arpeggio mark or arpeggiation sign.

An arpeggio is the playing of a chord's notes one at a time in rapid succession, rather than all simultaneously. It produces a flowing, wave-like sound that's more lyrical and expressive than a block chord. It can go up, down, or both. It's also known as a broken chord. Arpeggios appear across virtually every instrument and every style of music — from classical piano to acoustic guitar to film scores — and they're one of the most fundamental technical tools a musician practices. Whether you hear them as a gentle roll on a piano, a cascading harp glissando, or a picked guitar ballad, you're hearing notes of a chord set free in time, one after the other.
1013: Arrabbiata simply means angry or furious. It describes a person (or animal) who is in a real, felt state of anger — not mild, quiet irritation, but genuine, visible anger. Think of a person with a raised voice, a clenched jaw, or a flushed face. That person is arrabbiata (if female) or arrabbiato (if male).
The Four Forms of This Adjective

In Italian, adjectives must match the gender and number of the noun they describe. So this single word has four forms, all meaning the same thing — angry:

  • Arrabbiato — one male person
  • Arrabbiata — one female person
  • Arrabbiati — multiple males, or a mixed group
  • Arrabbiate — multiple females

A man says: "Sono arrabbiato." (I am angry.)
A woman says: "Sono arrabbiata." (I am angry.)
A group of people: "Sono arrabbiati." (They are angry.)

This is the standard rule for Italian adjectives, not something unusual about this particular word.

This is important. Arrabbiato/a is not a mild word. It sits firmly in the real, meaningful anger zone. Here is a rough emotional scale to place it on:

  • Seccato/a → slightly annoyed, like when someone interrupts you
  • Infastidito/a → bothered, irritated
  • Arrabbiato/a → genuinely angry, noticeable to others
  • Furioso/a → furious, barely-in-control rage

So "arrabbiato/a" is stronger than mere annoyance, but it does not necessarily suggest someone has lost all control. It covers the wide middle ground of real, human, everyday anger — the kind you feel when someone breaks a promise, cuts you off in traffic, or unfairly blames you for something.

In English, the closest words are: angry, mad (American usage), cross (British usage), or enraged.
How to Use It in a Sentence

The adjective is most commonly used in two positions:

1. After a verb (most common)
Here it follows verbs like essere (to be) or sembrare (to seem):

  • "Marco è arrabbiato." — Marco is angry.
  • "Sembra arrabbiata." — She seems angry.

2. Before or after a noun

  • "Un bambino arrabbiato." — An angry child.
  • "Un'arrabbiata cliente." — An angry (female) customer. (less common)

The far more natural and frequent pattern in everyday Italian is to use it predicatively (after a verb), not directly next to the noun.
Key Prepositions to Use With It

When you want to specify who the anger is directed at, or what caused it, you pair the adjective with these prepositions:

Con (with) — when angry at a person

  • "Sono arrabbiata con te." — I am angry with you.
  • "È arrabbiato con suo fratello." — He is angry with his brother.

Per (for / because of) — when angry about something

  • "È arrabbiata per il ritardo." — She is angry about the delay.
  • "Sono arrabbiato per quello che hai detto." — I am angry about what you said.

The adjective often appears alongside these verbs in real speech:

  • Essere (to be): "Sei arrabbiato?" — Are you angry?
  • Diventare (to become): "È diventata arrabbiata all'improvviso." — She suddenly became angry.
  • Sembrare (to seem): "Sembra molto arrabbiato." — He seems very angry.
  • Restare / Rimanere (to remain/stay): "È rimasta arrabbiata per giorni." — She stayed angry for days.

The related reflexive verb arrabbiarsi means "to get angry / to become angry" — this is the action, while arrabbiato/a is the resulting state.
The Famous Sauce — Your Best Memory Hook

If you have ever seen penne all'arrabbiata on an Italian menu, you already know this word. The sauce — made with tomatoes, garlic, olive oil, and fiery red chili peppers — is literally called the "angry" sauce. The logic is wonderfully simple: the burning heat of the chili peppers is described as rage. The sauce is so spicy, so fierce, that Italians said it was angry.

This is a perfect mnemonic: whenever you cannot remember what arrabbiato/a means, picture that blazing red pasta sauce burning your mouth — it's so hot it's furious.

Arrabbiato/a is an everyday, colloquial word. It is the natural word that Italians use in conversation, text messages, family arguments, and casual writing. In very formal or literary contexts, synonyms like irato/a or adirato/a (both meaning angry/irate) might appear instead — but in real, living Italian, arrabbiato/a is what you will hear and what you should use.

• What it means: Angry, furious, enraged
  • Who it describes: Primarily people (or animals), and metaphorically fierce things (like spicy sauce)
  • How strong: Real, visible anger — stronger than annoyance, less absolute than "furious"
  • Forms: Arrabbiato / Arrabbiata / Arrabbiati / Arrabbiate — always match the gender and number
  • Most common pattern: "Sono arrabbiato/a" — I am angry
  • To say angry at someone: add con — "arrabbiata con lui" (angry with him)
  • To say angry about something: add per — "arrabbiato per questo" (angry about this)
  • Style: Everyday, spoken Italian — completely natural in any normal conversation
1014:
To arraign someone means to formally bring them before a court of law and officially charge them with a crime — and then ask them, right there in front of the judge, whether they are guilty or not guilty.

Think of it as the moment the legal system officially and publicly says to a person: "Here is exactly what you are accused of doing. How do you respond?"

When someone is arraigned, three specific things happen in that courtroom:

  1. The charges are read out loud — the accused person hears, in precise legal language, exactly what crime they are being charged with.
  2. The accused enters a plea — they formally say "guilty," "not guilty," or sometimes "no contest" (meaning they don't admit guilt but also don't fight the charge).
  3. The judge decides on bail — whether the person can go home while waiting for trial, and under what conditions.

This is why arraignment is often called the first major step in a criminal trial. It's not the investigation, not the arrest, not the trial itself — it is the formal, official, on-the-record beginning of the court process.

The court (or the state, acting through a judge or magistrate) arraigns the accused person (also called the defendant).

You would say:

  • "The judge arraigned the suspect on three counts of fraud."
  • "He was arraigned this morning and pleaded not guilty."
  • "She will be arraigned before the district court on Monday."

Notice that the subject doing the arraigning is always a court or legal authority — not a police officer, not a victim, not a lawyer. The power to arraign belongs specifically to the judicial system.

Imagine you're playing a board game, and before any moves are made, the referee stops the game, reads the rule you allegedly broke in front of everyone, and asks you directly: "Did you break this rule? Yes or no?" That formal, official, face-to-face moment of accusation and required response — that's the spirit of what "arraign" means in a courtroom.

Outside of courtrooms, arraign can also be used figuratively to mean to accuse someone publicly, or to criticize and call someone to account for their actions — especially in a serious or formal way.

For example:

  • "The journalist arraigned the politicians for their years of corruption."
  • "He was arraigned by the public for his failure to act."

Here, it means something close to "publicly condemn" or "formally accuse" — but without the actual legal proceedings. This usage is more formal and literary, and you'll mostly see it in serious writing, speeches, or journalism. It carries a strong sense of moral accountability, not just personal criticism.

It helps to know what arraign is not, so you don't confuse it with nearby legal concepts:

  • Arrest → when police physically take someone into custody. This happens before arraignment.
  • Indictment → when a grand jury formally decides there is enough evidence to charge someone. This happens before arraignment too.
  • Arraignment → the court appearance where the charges are officially stated and the plea is entered. This comes after arrest and indictment.
  • Trial → where guilt is actually determined. This comes after arraignment.

So the sequence is: Arrest → Charge/Indictment → Arraignment → Trial → Verdict.

FormExample
Arraign (verb)They will arraign him tomorrow.
Arraigned (past tense)She was arraigned last Tuesday.
Arraignment (noun)The arraignment is scheduled for 9 a.m.
Arraigner (noun, rare)The entity arraigning the defendant.

To arraign someone is to formally bring them before a court, state the criminal charges against them on the record, and require them to declare whether they are guilty or not — and in a broader sense, it can also mean to publicly and seriously hold someone accountable for wrongdoing.
1015:
An arraignment is an official court hearing — one of the very first steps in the criminal justice process — where a person who has been charged with a crime is brought before a judge, told formally and on the record exactly what crime(s) they are accused of, and asked to respond by stating whether they are guilty or not guilty.

Think of it as the moment the legal system officially "opens the file" on a person and says: "Here are the charges against you. How do you respond?"
The Big Picture: Where It Fits

To understand arraignment fully, you need to see where it sits in the sequence of events:

  1. A crime is committed.
  2. Police investigate and make an arrest.
  3. The prosecutor formally files criminal charges.
  4. The accused person is brought to court for the arraignment. ← This is where the word lives.
  5. Later comes pre-trial hearings, possibly a trial, and then a verdict.

So the arraignment is not the trial. It is not where guilt is decided. It is simply the formal, official moment where the accused person hears the charges against them and officially responds to them, in a courtroom, in front of a judge. It is essentially the starting gun of the formal court process.
What Actually Happens at an Arraignment

An arraignment is a relatively short hearing. Here is what takes place during it:

1. The Charges Are Read Aloud

The judge or court clerk reads out the specific criminal charges against the accused person. This is not just a formality — it is a legal requirement. The law insists that every accused person must be clearly told, in open court, exactly what they are accused of doing and which law they allegedly broke. This protects people from being held or tried for vague, unnamed, or secret accusations.

2. Rights Are Confirmed

The judge confirms that the accused person is aware of their legal rights. This includes the right to have an attorney represent them. If the person cannot afford a lawyer, the court is required to provide one (called a public defender) at no cost to them. This too happens at or before the arraignment.

3. The Accused Enters a Plea

This is the heart of the arraignment. The accused person must respond to the charges by entering one of three pleas:

  • Guilty — "I did it. I accept responsibility." By pleading guilty, the person admits to the crime and skips the trial. The case then moves directly toward sentencing (deciding the punishment).
  • Not Guilty — "I did not do it, or I dispute these charges." This is by far the most common plea at arraignment, even among people who may eventually plead guilty later. Pleading not guilty simply means: "I am not accepting these charges right now. Let the process continue." It keeps all options open.
  • No Contest (also called "Nolo Contendere") — "I am not admitting guilt, but I will not fight the charge either." This is a unique middle-ground plea. The person is not saying they did it, but they are accepting the legal consequence (punishment) without a trial. It is often used when the accused wants to avoid the charge being used against them in a separate civil lawsuit, because a "no contest" plea cannot be treated as an admission of guilt in civil court the way a "guilty" plea can.

4. Bail Is Decided

The judge also decides at this stage whether the accused person will be held in jail until their trial or released. This decision involves setting bail — a sum of money the accused deposits with the court as a guarantee that they will show up to future hearings. If they do, they get the money back. If they flee, they forfeit it. In some cases, the judge may release the person without requiring any bail (called being released "on their own recognizance"), or may deny bail entirely if the person is considered dangerous or a flight risk.

5. Future Dates Are Set

The judge schedules the next court date — for example, a pre-trial hearing or, eventually, the trial itself.

At an arraignment, you will typically find:

  • The Judge — who runs the hearing and makes decisions.
  • The Defendant — the person accused of the crime.
  • The Defense Attorney — the lawyer representing the defendant.
  • The Prosecutor — the government's lawyer, who is arguing that the defendant should face the charges.
  • A Court Clerk — who handles the official paperwork and recording.

Because arraignment is one of several early legal proceedings, it gets confused with others. Here is how to keep them separate:

  • Arraignment ≠ Arrest. An arrest is when police detain you. An arraignment is a formal court hearing that comes later.
  • Arraignment ≠ Indictment. An indictment is a formal document (issued by a grand jury) that officially charges someone with a crime. The arraignment is the hearing in response to those charges — it is what happens after the indictment.
  • Arraignment ≠ Trial. The trial is where evidence is presented and guilt or innocence is determined. The arraignment happens long before the trial and has nothing to do with proving guilt. No witnesses are called. No evidence is examined.
  • Arraignment ≠ Preliminary Hearing. A preliminary hearing (in some systems) is where a judge decides if there is enough evidence to even justify putting the defendant on trial. An arraignment is simply about reading charges and getting a plea.

The arraignment serves several important purposes in a fair justice system:

  1. It ensures transparency. The accused cannot be held in legal limbo without being told what they are accused of. The charges must be stated openly.
  2. It ensures the accused has representation. The system checks that the person has a lawyer before anything serious proceeds.
  3. It sets the official legal direction. The plea entered at arraignment shapes everything that follows. A guilty plea leads to sentencing. A not-guilty plea leads to a trial.
  4. It protects rights. The entire proceeding is a safeguard against the government quietly holding or prosecuting someone without formal, public, documented process.

Imagine someone is arrested on suspicion of robbing a store. A few days later, the prosecutor files charges of "armed robbery." The accused is then brought into court for the arraignment. The judge says: "You are charged with armed robbery under Section X of the law. How do you plead?" The defendant's lawyer says: "Not guilty, Your Honor." The judge sets bail at $50,000 and schedules the next hearing for three weeks later. The arraignment is over in under 30 minutes.

That is all an arraignment is — a structured, formal, legally required moment where the accused hears the charges and officially responds, so that the machinery of justice can move forward in an orderly, rights-protecting way.
1016:
Arrant means complete, total, and absolute — but here's the critical catch: it is only ever used with bad or negative things. It's a word that takes something already negative and cranks it up to the maximum possible degree. Think of it as a supercharger for negative qualities.

When you call something arrant, you are saying: "This is not just bad. This is the worst, most extreme, most thorough version of this bad thing that you can imagine. There is nothing left out. It is 100% this."
The Key Feature That Makes It Special

In English, words like complete, total, utter, sheer, downright can also mean "absolute" — but they can go with both positive and negative things. You can say "a complete success" or "a complete failure." You can say "utter joy" or "utter chaos."

Arrant cannot do this. You will never hear "arrant brilliance" or "arrant kindness." The word is exclusively devoted to negativity — to faults, flaws, vices, and bad qualities. This is what makes it sharp and distinctive. When you see it, you instantly know that what follows is something negative, taken to its absolute extreme.

Let's go through several real uses, and for each one, break down exactly what the word is doing:

"That is arrant nonsense."

This doesn't just mean the idea is wrong or silly. It means the idea is completely, thoroughly, and totally without sense — not even a grain of truth, logic, or merit survives. The speaker is wiping it out entirely.

"He is an arrant coward."

This is not saying the person is somewhat cowardly or often cowardly. It's saying cowardice defines this person to the fullest possible degree. There is no bravery hiding anywhere. He is a coward through and through, completely and without exception.

"She told arrant lies."

These weren't half-truths or exaggerations. These were lies in the purest, most complete sense — deliberate, total, shameless falsehoods.

"The plan was arrant folly."

The plan wasn't just unwise or risky. It was thoroughly, absolutely, and completely foolish — folly of the highest order, with no trace of wisdom or good judgment to be found anywhere in it.

"He is an arrant knave."

A knave is a dishonest, unscrupulous person. Calling someone an arrant knave says he is not merely somewhat dishonest — he is a knave in the fullest, most complete sense of the word.

Arrant is not a neutral, dry word. It carries a tone of strong judgment, contempt, or exasperation. When someone uses it, they are not calmly describing something — they are expressing that something is outrageously bad, to a degree that deserves emphasis and strong condemnation.

It has a slightly formal, literary feel to it. You're more likely to encounter it in writing — in novels, essays, journalism, speeches — than in everyday casual conversation. But when a person does use it in speech, it sounds deliberate and forceful, like someone who means exactly what they're saying and wants you to feel the full weight of it.
What Kinds of Words Pair With It

Arrant almost always sits in front of nouns referring to:

  • Negative personal qualities: fool, coward, liar, hypocrite, villain, scoundrel, knave
  • Bad ideas or statements: nonsense, folly, rubbish, absurdity
  • Dishonest or immoral behavior: theft, fraud, deception

It will never sit in front of positive nouns. If you ever feel tempted to write "arrant genius" or "arrant beauty" — stop. That's not how the word works.
A Simple Test to Know When to Use It

Ask yourself three questions before using arrant:

  1. Is the thing I'm describing negative? ✅ Required.
  2. Is it total and without exception — not just partial or occasional? ✅ Required.
  3. Am I making a strong judgment about it — not just neutrally noting it? ✅ Required.

If all three answers are yes, arrant is likely the right word.
Summing It Up in One Sentence

Arrant means complete and absolute — but reserved exclusively for negative qualities, always implying that the thing in question is thoroughly and without exception bad, to the fullest possible degree.
1017:
Array means a collection of things arranged in an organized, ordered way — and often an impressive one. It's not just a random pile or a simple list. An array has a sense of purposeful arrangement and usually notable size or variety.

Think of it this way: if you dumped a box of crayons on the floor, that's a mess. But if you laid them out neatly in a line from red to violet, each in its place — that's an array.
Meaning 1: An Impressive and Ordered Collection (Everyday Use)

This is the most common way the word is used in everyday English.

When someone says "an array of something," they mean a wide, well-organized, and often striking set of options, things, or choices.

Examples:

  • "The buffet had an array of dishes from around the world."
  • "She walked into the store and faced a dazzling array of shoes."
  • "The hospital offers an array of treatment options."

Notice that the word carries a subtle sense of being impressed by the quantity or variety. You wouldn't say "an array of two things." The word implies enough variety or quantity to be noteworthy.

The nuance: Unlike a simple "collection" or "group," array suggests that the things are spread out visibly and in order, almost like a display laid out for you to see and appreciate.

In military and historical contexts, an array refers to troops arranged in battle order — soldiers lined up in a deliberate, strategic formation, ready for combat.

Example:

  • "The general surveyed his array of soldiers before the battle began."

Here, the sense of organized arrangement is even stronger — every soldier is in their exact, intentional position.

In mathematics, an array is a rectangular arrangement of numbers, symbols, or objects in rows and columns.

Imagine a grid:

```
1 2 3
4 5 6
7 8 9
```

This 3×3 grid is an array. Each item has a specific position defined by which row and which column it sits in. Arrays are used to organize data so that mathematical operations can be performed on them neatly and systematically.

This is one of the most important uses of the word today. In programming, an array is a data structure — a way of storing multiple values in a single, organized container, where each value sits at a specific numbered position called an index.

Think of it like a row of numbered lockers:

```
Locker 0: "Alice"
Locker 1: "Bob"
Locker 2: "Charlie"
```

You can instantly reach into locker number 2 and get "Charlie." You don't have to search through everything — you just go straight to the position you want.

Key properties of an array in computing:

  • The items are stored in a fixed, sequential order.
  • Each item has a numbered index (usually starting from 0).
  • You access any item by referring to its index number.
  • Arrays are typically used to store items of the same type (e.g., all numbers, or all names).

Example:

  • A list of the 7 days of the week stored as an array: ["Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday"]
  • To get "Wednesday," you ask for index 2.

Arrays are one of the most fundamental building blocks in programming because they allow you to work with many pieces of data efficiently under a single name.
Meaning 5: In Science (Antenna or Telescope Arrays)

In physics and astronomy, an array refers to a group of devices — such as antennas, telescopes, or sensors — arranged together and working as a single, unified system.

Example:

  • A radio telescope array is a set of many individual radio dishes spread across a large area. Together, they act like one giant telescope far more powerful than any single dish could be.
  • The Very Large Array (VLA) in New Mexico is a famous example — 27 large antennas arranged in a Y-shaped pattern to observe radio waves from space.

The logic is the same: individual units, arranged purposefully, working together as one.

In older literature and poetry, array was used to mean clothing, especially fine or splendid clothing — the way someone is dressed or adorned.

Example:

  • "The queen appeared in magnificent array." (meaning: dressed in grand, glorious clothing)

You'll mostly encounter this in classic literature, the Bible, or formal/poetic writing. It is rarely used this way in modern everyday speech.
The Thread That Ties All Meanings Together

No matter which context you encounter the word in, array always carries the same two ideas at its core:

  1. Multiplicity — there are many items, not just one.
  2. Order — they are arranged with purpose and structure, not scattered randomly.

And in most uses, there's also a quiet third quality: impressiveness — an array is usually large enough or varied enough to catch your attention.
Quick Contrast: Array vs. Similar Words

• Array vs. Collection: A collection is just "things gathered together." An array adds the sense of organized arrangement and often impressiveness.
  • Array vs. List: A list is sequential and often informal. An array (especially in computing and math) is a formal, structured, indexed arrangement.
  • Array vs. Group: A group has no implication of order at all. An array always does.

In short: whenever you see the word array, picture things laid out carefully and deliberately — in clear view, in order, and in impressive number or variety. That image will serve you well across every context where this word appears.
1018:
To array something means to arrange it in a neat, orderly, and often visually impressive way — deliberately, with purpose. Think of it as arranging things so they can be clearly seen, properly organized, or used effectively.

The key feeling behind this word is intentional, ordered display. You don't just throw things together. You lay them out thoughtfully.

1. To arrange objects or people in an orderly or impressive manner

This is the most common use. When things are arrayed, they are spread out, lined up, or positioned in a deliberate way — often to create a powerful or striking effect.

The general arrayed his troops along the hilltop.

This means the general carefully positioned his soldiers in a deliberate formation — not randomly, but with strategy and order.

She arrayed the plates, glasses, and cutlery on the dining table.

Here, she arranged them carefully and properly, not just tossed them around.

The products were arrayed neatly on the store shelves.

Lined up, organized, presented well.

Notice the pattern: things that are arrayed are always deliberately placed and usually spread out in some way so that they are visible, accessible, or impressive.

2. To dress someone in fine, special, or splendid clothing

This meaning is older and more literary. When a person is arrayed in clothing, they are dressed up — usually in something grand, ceremonial, or beautiful. You'll often see this in classical literature, religious texts, or formal writing.

The queen was arrayed in silk robes and golden jewels.

She was dressed in them — adorned, clothed in something magnificent.

The priests were arrayed in white garments for the ceremony.

They were dressed in ceremonial clothing.

In this sense, the word carries a sense of dignity and splendor. People aren't just wearing clothes — they are presented in them, almost like they are being displayed.
The Thread That Connects Both Meanings

Both meanings share the same underlying idea: a deliberate, careful, and often impressive arrangement — whether it's objects on a table, soldiers on a battlefield, or a person dressed in fine clothing. In every case, something is being put into order with intention and care.
The Register: When Is This Word Used?

"Array" as a verb is formal and literary. You won't often hear it in casual everyday conversation. It appears more in:

  • Literature and classic novels
  • Military or historical writing
  • Formal or ceremonial descriptions
  • Journalism that aims for an elevated, impressive tone

In everyday speech, people would more likely say arrange, line up, lay out, dress, or clothe — but "array" carries a more powerful, elegant, and deliberate feeling than any of those.
How It Differs from Similar Words

• Arrange is the closest everyday equivalent, but it is neutral and plain. Array implies something more purposeful and often more impressive in scale or appearance.
  • Display focuses on showing something to others; array focuses on how the things are organized and positioned.
  • Dress (for the clothing meaning) is simple and everyday. Array suggests grandeur and ceremony.

SituationWhat "array" means

In short:

  • Arranging things/people → to position them in a deliberate, orderly, and often striking way.
  • Dressing someone → to clothe them in fine, impressive garments.

Both uses carry a sense of care, order, and impressiveness. If you see or use the word array as a verb, it is never casual or accidental — something is always being placed, organized, or presented with intention.
1019:
Arrears (always used in plural form) refers to money that was supposed to be paid by a certain time, but wasn't. It is the unpaid amount that has piled up because someone fell behind on their financial obligations.

Think of it this way: you have a debt, it has a due date, the due date passes, and you still haven't paid. That unpaid, overdue amount is called "arrears."

You will almost never see the word "arrears" standing alone. It almost always appears in the phrase "in arrears." This phrase simply means behind on payments.

It can describe a person or an account:

  • "She is in arrears on her rent." → She owes rent she hasn't paid yet.
  • "His loan account is in arrears." → He has missed payments on his loan.
Common Contexts Where You'll See This Word

Arrears can build up in many financial situations:

  • Rent arrears — A tenant owes unpaid rent to a landlord.
  • Mortgage arrears — A homeowner has missed home loan payments.
  • Tax arrears — Someone owes taxes to the government that are overdue.
  • Child support arrears — A parent owes court-ordered child support payments they haven't made.
  • Wage/salary arrears — An employer owes employees money for work already done but not yet paid.
  • Utility bill arrears — Unpaid electricity, water, or gas bills that are overdue.
Important: "Arrears" Always Refers to the Past

This is a crucial detail. Arrears always points backward in time. The obligation already existed. The deadline already passed. The money was already supposed to be paid. What remains unpaid is the arrears.

It is not about future debt. It is about debt that is already overdue.
"Arrears" Can Also Refer to a Specific Amount

Arrears isn't just a condition — it can also refer to the actual sum of money that is overdue.

  • "He owed $4,500 in arrears." → The total amount he is behind on is $4,500.
  • "She finally cleared her arrears." → She paid off all the overdue money she owed.

Fall into arrears — to begin missing payments; to go from being up-to-date to being behind.

"After losing his job, he quickly fell into arrears on his mortgage."

Be in arrears — to currently be behind on payments.

"The company is in arrears on several supplier invoices."

Clear/pay off the arrears — to pay back everything that is overdue and get back on track.

"It took her two years to clear the arrears on her student loan."

Fall further into arrears — the situation is getting worse; the unpaid amount keeps growing.

"Without income, he fell further into arrears each month."
A Special, Neutral Use: "Paid in Arrears"

This is an important case where "arrears" does not have a negative meaning. In employment and business, "paid in arrears" simply means that payment is made after the work or service has been completed — not before.

For example: if you work a full week (Monday to Friday) and receive your paycheck the following week, you are being paid in arrears. This is actually the standard practice for most jobs in the world. It just means you work first, then get paid — as opposed to being paid in advance.

So in this context, "paid in arrears" is neutral and simply describes the timing of payment, not a failure to pay.

"Arrears" is always plural, even when referring to a single situation or a single unpaid amount. You never say "an arrear." It always takes a plural verb:

  • ✅ "The arrears are significant."
  • ❌ "The arrears is significant."

This is similar to words like goods, savings, or wages — always plural in form.
The Emotional Weight of the Word

In everyday life, being "in arrears" signals financial trouble. It can trigger serious consequences: eviction, legal action, credit score damage, wage garnishment, or penalties. It often appears in formal letters, legal documents, court rulings, and financial statements. So when you encounter this word, understand that it carries a sense of urgency — something is overdue and needs to be resolved.
Arrears is the unpaid, overdue money that someone owes because they have fallen behind on a financial obligation — and "in arrears" means being in that state of being behind.
